reference.source: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
clinicalPearls: A true Jones fracture lies at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction of the fifth metatarsal (zone 2), extending into the fourth-fifth intermetatarsal articulation, whereas the more distal zone-3 diaphyseal stress fracture lies beyond that joint
This zone sits at a vascular watershed, predisposing to delayed union and non-union
It must be distinguished from a proximal tuberosity avulsion (pseudo-Jones, zone 1), which usually heals well with symptomatic treatment
The typical mechanism is an adduction or inversion load on a plantarflexed foot, or repetitive stress in athletes
Acute fractures may be managed with non-weight-bearing cast immobilisation, but intramedullary screw fixation is often preferred in athletes and high-demand patients
Chronic zone 3 proximal diaphyseal stress fractures show sclerosis and medullary narrowing and behave differently
Careful attention to which zone is involved directs both prognosis and management
reference.pathophysiology: The proximal fifth metatarsal has a zonal blood supply, and the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction (zone 2) lies at a watershed between the metaphyseal vessels and the nutrient artery supplying the diaphysis. Fractures in this relatively poorly perfused region heal slowly and are prone to delayed and non-union, in contrast to the well-vascularised tuberosity where avulsion fractures unite readily. Tensile and bending forces transmitted through the lateral border of the foot during adduction or inversion, or accumulated microdamage from repetitive loading, exceed the bone's capacity to remodel, producing an acute fracture or a chronic stress fracture.
additionalDifferentials: Unfused apophysis or os vesalianum in skeletally immature patients
additionalInvestigations: Anteroposterior, oblique and lateral foot radiographs to localise the fracture zone
Weight-bearing views to assess alignment and stability
Comparison of fracture position against the tuberosity and intermetatarsal joint
CT to evaluate suspected non-union or medullary sclerosis
MRI for early diagnosis of stress fracture before radiographic change
redFlags: Established non-union with sclerosis and obliteration of the medullary canal
Recurrent or refractory fracture in an athlete
Misclassification of the fracture zone altering prognosis and treatment
Persistent pain despite immobilisation suggesting failure of union
reference.prognosis: True zone 2 Jones fractures have notable rates of delayed and non-union owing to their watershed blood supply, whereas proximal tuberosity avulsions generally heal uneventfully; surgical fixation improves and speeds union in high-demand patients.
pitfalls: Confusing a proximal tuberosity avulsion (pseudo-Jones) with a true Jones fracture
Permitting early weight-bearing that promotes non-union
Failing to recognise chronic stress-fracture features on radiographs
Not counselling athletes about the option and benefits of early fixation
references: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
management: Treat acute fractures with non-weight-bearing cast or boot immobilisation, recognising the watershed blood supply predisposes to slow union
Offer intramedullary screw fixation for athletes, high-demand patients and displaced fractures to speed and secure union
Optimise bone healing by correcting vitamin D and calcium status, and advising smoking cessation
Monitor union radiographically given the substantial risk of delayed and non-union at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction
Manage established non-union with revision fixation and bone grafting, with adjunctive bone stimulation where appropriate
Guide graded return to loading with lateral-column offloading orthotics and rehabilitation
Escalate to surgical fixation if conservative treatment fails to progress to union
